transcript.text: Hi, my Hotpoint Aquarius dryer is taking forever to dry and the top gets really hot. Model is TCM580GUK if that helps

A Hotpoint Aquarius TCM580GUK that takes a long time to dry and gets very hot on top is most often suffering from restricted airflow. When the air can't flow freely through the lint filter or condenser, the dryer overheats (hence the hot top) and the clothes don't dry properly because the moist air isn't being expelled effectively. Before we look at internal parts, please check these two simple things:
1. Is the main fluff filter (usually in the door frame) completely clean?
2. If your model has a condenser unit (often behind a flap at the bottom front), is that also clear of lint and debris? Also, which programme are you running? Some 'cool air' or 'refresh' cycles do not use heat, so if you're on one of those, it will take much longer to dry.

Thanks for the quick reply. The fluff filter in the door has a thick layer of fluff on it, I'll admit I sometimes forget to clean it. The condenser at the bottom front had lint packed on the fins, so I rinsed it and it looks much cleaner now. I'm not sure which programme I was using, I'm afraid. Also, the top panel gets very hot and I often run the dryer while I'm out at work.

The hot top and slow drying strongly suggest restricted airflow. Please check the vent hose at the back of the dryer: ensure it isn’t kinked or squashed, and clear any lint from it. Also, if your model vents to the outside, check the wall vent for a fluff buildup. If the hose is clear but it still doesn't dry properly after this, we may need to look at whether the thermal cut-out has tripped.
I'm not sure how to check that, I'm afraid. Mine is a condenser dryer, so I wasn't aware it had a vent hose or a wall vent. Is there something else I can check on it?

Since the airflow blockage has been cleared but the drying is still poor and it gets very hot, the dryer's internal safety thermostat (the thermal cut-out) may have tripped to prevent a fire and is now cutting off the heat. To check if this is the case: please run a standard 'Cottons' or 'Normal Dry' programme for about 10 minutes. Carefully feel the air coming out of the condenser area (or near the door); it should be quite warm or hot. If the air remains cool while the drum tumbles, the heater isn't working, which suggests a failed component like the thermal cut-out or heater element that will need an engineer to replace.

I haven't done that exact test, I'm afraid, and I'm not confident judging the air temperature from the condenser area. I can say the drum turns and the dryer does heat, since the top panel gets very hot. There's also a faint warm, dusty smell in the utility room, though it isn't a strong burning smell. Do you think it's safe to keep using it in the meantime?

No, it is not safe to leave the dryer running while you are out at work. The combination of an extremely hot top panel and a dusty/burning smell suggests the appliance is overheating, possibly because the airflow restriction has tripped a safety thermostat or because a heating component is failing. This presents a genuine fire risk. Please stop using it immediately and arrange for a qualified engineer to inspect it.

candidates: Blocked airflow (lint filter or condenser) causing overheating and poor drying (high)
Faulty heating element or thermal cut-out (medium)
